source_refs.note: Book p. 67-69: matrix inversion method, Example 12

blocks.text: The matrix inversion method is a way to solve a system of linear equations using the inverse of a matrix.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The idea in three lines. Write the system as \(AX = B\). If \(|A| \ne 0\), multiply both sides on the left by \(A^{-1}\):
\[A^{-1}(AX) = A^{-1}B\]
\[(A^{-1}A)X = A^{-1}B\]
\[X = A^{-1}B\]
because \(A^{-1}A = I\) and \(IX = X\). It is the matrix version of solving \(ax = b\) as \(x = \frac{b}{a}\).
\(A^{-1}\) must be on the LEFT of \(B\); matrix multiplication is not commutative, and \(BA^{-1}\) is not even defined here.
We find \(A^{-1}\) by \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\) (Section 4.5) or by row operations (Section 4.7).

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem:
Use matrix inversion method to solve the system
\[x_1 - 2x_2 + x_3 = -4\]
\[2x_1 - 3x_2 + 2x_3 = -6\]
\[2x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 5\]
steps:
Given: the system of three equations in \(x_1, x_2, x_3\).
To find: \(x_1, x_2, x_3\).
Method: write the system as \(AX = B\); if \(|A| \ne 0\), then \(X = A^{-1}B\), with \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\).

Step 1: Matrix form
\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -6 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\]
or \(AX = B\) ...(i), where
\[A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix},\ B = \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -6 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: the coefficients of each equation form a row of \(A\); the constants form \(B\).

Step 2: Find \(|A|\)
\(R_2 + (-2)R_1 \to R_2'\):
\[|A| = \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\]
Expanding by \(R_2\):
\[= (-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (1 - 2) = -1\]
Why: this row operation does not change the determinant and makes \(R_2 = (0, 1, 0)\), so the expansion has only one term. \(|A| \ne 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists and (i) can be written as \(X = A^{-1}B\) ...(ii).

Step 3: Cofactors of the first row
\[A_{11} = +\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} = -3 - 4 = -7\]
\[A_{12} = -\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} = -(2 - 4) = 2\]
\[A_{13} = +\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} = 4 + 6 = 10\]
Why: \(A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\), where the minor \(M_{ij}\) is the determinant left after deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\).

Step 4: Cofactors of the second and third rows
\[A_{21} = -\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} = -(-2 - 2) = 4\]
\[A_{22} = +\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} = 1 - 2 = -1\]
\[A_{23} = -\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} = -(2 + 4) = -6\]
\[A_{31} = +\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{vmatrix} = -4 + 3 = -1\]
\[A_{32} = -\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} = -(2 - 2) = 0\]
\[A_{33} = +\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{vmatrix} = -3 + 4 = 1\]
Why: the sign pattern for rows 2 and 3 is \(-, +, -\) and \(+, -, +\). So
\[[A_{ij}]_{3\times 3} = \begin{bmatrix}-7 & 2 & 10 \\ 4 & -1 & -6 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]

Step 5: Adjoint and inverse
\[\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix}-7 & 4 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 10 & -6 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
\[A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = \frac{1}{-1}\operatorname{adj} A\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -10 & 6 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix (rows become columns). Dividing by \(|A| = -1\) changes every sign.

Step 6: Multiply \(A^{-1}B\)
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -10 & 6 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -6 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}-28 + 24 + 5 \\ 8 - 6 + 0 \\ 40 - 36 - 5\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: each entry is a row of \(A^{-1}\) times the column \(B\): for example \(7(-4) + (-4)(-6) + 1(5) = 1\).

Check: substitute \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 2, x_3 = -1\):
\[1 - 4 - 1 = -4\]
\[2 - 6 - 2 = -6\]
\[2 + 4 - 1 = 5\]
All three equations hold.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Write the system as \(AX = B\).
2. Check \(|A| \ne 0\); otherwise the method cannot be used.
3. \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\), where \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.
4. \(X = A^{-1}B\), with \(A^{-1}\) on the left.
5. Check by substituting into the original equations.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix when writing \(\operatorname{adj} A\).
2. Wrong cofactor signs: use the chessboard pattern \(+, -, +\) / \(-, +, -\) / \(+, -, +\).
3. Writing \(X = BA^{-1}\). The product must be \(A^{-1}B\).
4. Forgetting to divide by \(|A|\) (here \(-1\), which changes every sign).
